chunks: However, this is as we have said,

we have proven the necessity of the Imam, because the aspect of need for him, which is continuous in every state and time, is that he is a grace for us, as discussed earlier, and no one else can take his place.
The need related to narration (hearing/transmission) is also clear,
because although the narration comes from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and the forefathers of the Imam (peace be upon them) regarding all that is needed in the jurisprudence,
it is possible for the reliable narrators to deviate from it, either intentionally or due to a doubt,
so the narration may become disconnected or remain through someone who is not reliable in his narration.
We have fully discussed this method in *Talkhis al-Shafi*, so we will not prolong by mentioning it in the book.
ai.seo_question: Why is the Imam necessary and how is religious knowledge transmitted reliably?
ai.summary: Al-Tusi highlights the Imam as a perpetual divine grace (lutf) whose presence is essential for guiding the community, distinguishing his infallible authority from the fallible transmission of hadith by narrators who may err or deviate. This passage underscores the Shia epistemological concern that while revelation is complete, its preservation relies on trustworthy transmitters, making the Imam's role as the ultimate guarantor of truth indispensable during the occultation. The reference to 'Takhjîm al-Shâfî' indicates this argument is part of a broader theological framework established by earlier scholars to counter doubts about religious authority in the absence of the visible Imam.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: However, the case is as we assert:
we proved the need of the Imam, because the reason of this need, which is continuous in every time and age, is that he is a grace for us, as discussed earlier, and no one can take his place.
The need of narration is also clear,
because though narrations are from the Prophet (s) and forefathers of the Imam (a.s),
it is possible that the narrators turn away from them, either intentionally or by mistake,
and the narration may remain disconnected or through someone who is not reliable.
We have discussed this fully in Talkhis Shafi and will not prolong the inquiry by bringing it here.
